reasoning: Set A is the stronger plan for a learn-by-building RL student. The pedagogy is sound: a tabular-to-DQN progression in Snake; a hand-written policy-gradient ladder with matched step budgets; a compass-DQN vs PPO comparison that shows why policy gradients exist; ablations of every key ingredient; fixed-opponent controls before co-training; co-training checkpoints scored against a fixed scripted yardstick; and a snapshot cross-play grid. Its acceptance criteria give exact numbers and arithmetic checks, which makes it highly testable. The build order (gated core extraction, then a staged project layout with config files listed per stage) makes the next step obvious. A loses points for size and stale text. The brief is still framed around Snake: its bets, its success line about Environment 2, and its Snake-specific bot wording in Goal 2. One idea file keeps an open question that AD-13 already answers. The architecture keeps history residue ('unchanged since the Snake stage') and a heavy three-generation protocol and adapter stack. It also treats timeouts as terminal and explicitly excludes reward shaping, a concept the user wants to learn. Set B is leaner, more readable and mostly consistent. It has good touches: truncation bootstrapping, Double DQN, notes and done reports. But its RL methodology is weaker. Wall-clock training budgets conflict with its own reproducibility requirement and make the SB3 comparison unfair. Success rests on a single training seed. Opponent sampling is described per episode in the spec and per rollout in the architecture. It claims SB3 settings 'match' when SB3's DQN has no Double-DQN targets and its PPO minibatch default differs. Many acceptance criteria are vague (no tank sizes or speeds, 'behaves as the world section describes'). It also brings library comparison into every world's done criteria, against the user's 'only later' preference, and skips the PG ladder and ablations that would help the user explain why things work.

strengths: Concept-driven progression: tabular Q then DQN in Snake; plain PG, baseline, actor-critic, then PPO in the tank, with equal step budgets (PG-08)
Compass-tank DQN beside PPO directly contrasts value-based and policy-gradient learning on the same task
Ablations (ABL-01..ABL-12) cover replay, target net, exploration decay, clipping, normalization, baseline, GAE, limited sight, alternating and pool, which serves 'explain why it works'
Arena design is RL-literate: fixed-opponent control runs, co-training checkpoints scored against fixed scripted bots (EVAL-10), and a snapshot cross-play grid with an escalation check
Acceptance criteria are concrete and numerically checkable (e.g. TAB-02 1.45, PG-07 (-1.22, 0, 1.22), sense vector sizes 10/19/20 all add up)
Staged project layout with per-stage files and configs, plus golden-run tests guarding earlier results
Keeps library comparison for later, matching the user's preference
weaknesses: Brief is still framed around Snake: bets, success criteria and Goal 2 wording are Snake-only, and Environment 3 is missing from success
Stale artifacts: an unresolved open question in ideas/predator-prey.md, a wrong CORE ID, and history phrasing in the architecture
Heavy for a solo hobby project: three protocol layers with stacked adapters; roughly 1,100 lines of docs
Timeouts treated as terminal (no truncation bootstrap) despite 1,000-step limits with per-step survival reward
Reward shaping explicitly out of scope although it is a target concept
Significance test admitted likely infeasible with 5 seeds and Holm over 10 tank comparisons, left as an open question
Plain-language substitutes ('spread', 'smoothed advantage estimates', 'ingredient removal') sometimes obscure standard terms

strengths: Concise and readable; brief, spec and architecture give the three worlds equal weight
A single multi-agent World protocol from day one keeps the core simple; shared worlds.physics module
Technically solid method details: Double DQN, Huber loss, GAE, and truncation bootstrapping via a separate 'truncated' flag
Done report and NOTE requirements make 'explain why it works' a concrete deliverable
Predator-prey balance levers (1.2x speed, 0.5x turn rate) and a snapshot pool for self-play
Honest risk list (VecEnv caught-fish slot difference, early-snapshot strength)
weaknesses: Wall-clock training budget (CORE-04) conflicts with bit-identical reproducibility (CORE-08) and makes the SB3 comparison depend on code speed
Success is decided from a single trained agent; no replication across training seeds
Library comparison is pulled into every world's done criteria, against the user's 'only later' preference
Incorrect parity claims with SB3 (no Double DQN in SB3's DQN; PPO minibatch default is 64, not 256)
Opponent sampling is per episode in the spec but per rollout in the architecture; independent per-side picks can freeze both sides; the empty pool at start is not handled
Many vague tests: no tank sizes, speeds or radii; 'behaves as the world section describes'; 'distinguishable at a glance'
Less learning depth: no tabular step, no PG ladder, no ablations; exploration and reward shaping are not studied

brief.md: "Environment 2 reuses the shared core without copying Snake code." — success criteria stop at Environment 2; Environment 3 is missing (stale two-environment framing)
brief.md: "they beat a random bot and a naive greedy bot that heads straight for food" — Goal 2 uses Snake-specific wording, but spec BASE serves Goal 2 in all three games
brief.md: "The next environment starts faster." — Goal 5 is phrased for one follow-on game, while CORE now spans three
spec.md: "Reward shaping in any game, and a shaping ablation." (out of scope) — the user lists reward shaping as a concept to learn

spec.md TAB-02: "When the episode ended, the target is the reward alone." — also applies to timeouts (SNAKE-06, the 1,000-step limits); no split between truncation and termination, so no bootstrap at the time limit
spec.md Open questions: "and certainly not for 10 in the tank" — the stated success test (EVAL-06) is admitted likely unpassable as specced and is left unresolved
spec.md PG-05: "which stand in the value estimate of the next state for the rest of the return" — garbled definition of GAE
spec.md TANK-08: "Given a fish at the centre of the tank ... the wall distance is 0.97" — 'direction to the nearest wall point' is undefined at the centre and has no edge case
ideas/predator-prey.md: "Should the arena share the tank's physics code through the core, or own a copy?" — still listed as open although AD-13 answers it (fish-tank.md says 'Resolved in the spec')
ideas/predator-prey.md: "CORE-04 (two learning sides)" — the two-side requirement is CORE-05
architecture.md: "single-agent seam (Snake implements these; unchanged since the Snake stage)" — history residue in the current-state document
architecture.md AD-08: "Since the arena stage, the core itself runs on TeamEnv" and "Gymnasium adapters ... wrap MultiEnv" — AD-08 is partly superseded by AD-11 but was patched rather than restated
architecture.md: "Snake reaches the core through as_team(as_multi(…))" — three protocol generations with stacked adapters, kept only to avoid editing Snake; too heavy for a solo learning lab

architecture.md AD-05: "Snake's 5 configurations, the tank's 10 and the arena's 5, each over 5 seeds" — 100 training runs of up to an hour each, likely more than 'a few weeks per environment' of evenings
B: spec.md CORE-04: "a 60-minute budget, when training is started, then it stops on its own within the budget" — conflicts with CORE-08 "the logged returns are identical"; how many steps fit in the time limit varies with machine load
spec.md EVAL-05: "the same 60-minute budget" — comparing against SB3 by wall-clock mixes implementation speed with sample efficiency

brief.md: "For Snake and the fish tank, my methods roughly match the established implementation." — makes library comparison a done criterion for each world; the user wants library comparison only later
architecture.md AD-08: "Settings are matched to AD-05 and AD-06" — SB3's DQN has no Double-DQN targets, so it cannot match AD-05
architecture.md AD-06: "10 epochs of minibatch 256 ... the defaults above match SB3's" — SB3 PPO's default minibatch is 64

spec.md PRED-10: "In each training episode, the opponent is the other side's current version half the time" vs architecture.md AD-07: "Each rollout picks, per side, the current opponent" — the granularity differs between docs

architecture.md AD-07: "Each rollout picks, per side, the current opponent with probability 0.5 ... A side learns only from rollouts where it plays its current policy" — independent per-side picks can freeze both sides; the empty pool before the first snapshot is not handled
spec.md VAL-05: "A Snake agent trained with this method ... passes EVAL-04" — success rests on one training run; no replication across training seeds
spec.md POL-03: "the size of each update is logged and stays within the configured limit on average" — PPO clipping does not bound update size this way; the test is vague
spec.md TANK-01/TANK-02: "The tank is a circle." / "The ball moves at constant speed" — no sizes, speeds or radii, so behavior is not falsifiable
spec.md TANK-08: "Given fish that survived 1,000, 1,000 and 400 steps (and others) ... the score is the average across all 8" — the test case is incomplete
spec.md EVAL-02: "then it behaves as the world section describes" — not a testable criterion
spec.md RPLY-02: "distinguishable at a glance" — subjective acceptance criterion
architecture.md: "Sensing uses a 13×13 pairwise distance matrix" — matches no world's body count (tank 9; predator-prey 9 animals plus 12 pellets)

brief.md: "each learned side beats a hand-written opponent and saved earlier versions of the other side" vs spec.md PRED-11, which compares the final side against its own matching early snapshot — the success definitions differ

spec.md Summary: "A world is done when its learned agent significantly beats random and hand-written baselines, can be watched ... and has a written note" — omits the reference-match criterion that the brief and EVAL-06 require

architecture.md AD-06: "REINFORCE or vanilla actor-critic — simpler to write, a great first step, but unstable" — the ladder is rejected, and with no ablations the learner has less material to explain why PPO works
